Article content The Brampton truck driver, accused of trying to smuggle 281 bricks of cocaine worth between $5 million and $34 million over the Blue Water Bridge last year, exchanged handshakes and a bro hug with his lawyers after hearing a Sarnia judge’s decision Thursday morning. Play Video Article content “Mr. Singh is hereby found not guilty of all charges,” Justice Mark Poland said after spending an hour explaining his verdicts. But the smile quickly turned to tears as he left the courtroom and the weight of the accusations, and how a double-digit prison sentence potentially had been on deck had the judge come back with a different decision, hit him. Singh was asked for comment after he had a chance to gather himself. “Whatever evidence they have proved their innocence. I am very happy, now,” Singh said. Defence lawyer Guruveer Sangha said he thought it was the right decision. “We believed he was innocent from Day 1 based on the evidence that the Crown had. We’re just happy the judge saw what we saw from the beginning,” he said. Advertisement 3 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Prosecutor Stephane Marinier said the judge provided thorough and thoughtful reasons. “That said, the Crown will review those reasons to determine whether or not to launch an appeal in the next 30 days,” he said. DISCOVERY OF THE DRUGS Singh, an Indian immigrant who came to Canada in 2022 on a student visa, was driving for Divine Freightlines Inc. and picked up a trailer loaded with pallets of plastic resin at Redhawk Logistics in Columbus, Ohio, mid-afternoon on March 5, 2025. On arrival at the bridge shortly after 11 p.m., his truck was sent for a mandatory inspection as it had been flagged by border officials. Officers found several black duffel bags between the skids holding large canvas sacks of resin. All 24 skids were unloaded, a drug-sniffing dog was brought in, and cocaine was found in seven of the 24 sacks. A total of 281, one-kilogram bricks of cocaine, which weighed 333 kilograms in the packaging, were found. Singh, then 23, was charged with importing cocaine and possessing cocaine for trafficking. He was freed on $200,000 bail two weeks later. Two Brampton men who run a trucking company later were charged with conspiracy to import drugs in this case. Article content A trial only for Singh, who pleaded not guilty to both charges he was facing, began earlier this year at the Sarnia courthouse. It was spread out over multiple weeks and was heard by Poland without a jury. After listening to both sides’ closing arguments, he adjourned the case to Thursday for his decision. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and RCMP said nearly 420 kilograms of cocaine worth $11 million was seized in trucks at the Blue Water Bridge during two drug-smuggling cases on Feb. 27 and March 6, 2025. (CBSA/RCMP) THE CROWN’S CASE Marinier argued there were three viable options for how the drugs got in the trailer: They were put there by the driver who brought the trailer to Columbus. They were put there by someone else during the roughly seven hours before Singh arrived. Singh picked them up from another driver and he drove them in his cab to Columbus and put them in the trailer when he got there. There was ample opportunity to get the cocaine from another trucker coming from California while he stayed overnight in the Hebron, Ky., Marinier argued. But, he added, he didn’t have to prove any of these theories, just that Singh knew the drugs were in his trailer. He argued the evidence showed Singh knew about them beyond a reasonable doubt. He also argued Singh moved the trailer’s axles before leaving Columbus because of the added weight of the drugs and Singh was deceitful with the border officers. Singh was roughly 150 kilometres away at the time. When he did arrive, he was only there for 37 minutes before leaving. His client also wasn’t nervous or evasive during the inspection, his fingerprints weren’t on the drugs, and police didn’t find any coded messages on his phone, Sangha said. He argued his client was an unwitting courier and the drugs were put there by other people who were working above him. Singh testified through a Punjabi interpreter during several days and denied knowing the drugs were in his trailer and Sangha argued the Crown didn’t prove his client had knowledge or was willfully blind. Trucks on the Blue Water Bridge near Sarnia. (File photo/The Observer) THE JUDGE’S REASONS While reading his hour-plus decision on the not guilty verdicts, Poland noted a major plank in the Crown’s case was a high valued shipment of drugs would only be entrusted to a person with knowledge of its existence, and there was a further suggestion that, as the value increases, the inference they would know about the drugs becomes proportionally stronger. Article content But the judge said that was unsupported by a significant amount of other compelling evidence. He also pointed out, as the value increases, the resources of the parties directing the shipment also goes up and they could possibly have a team of unobserved handlers following the shipment. Additionally, using a blind courier could have certain advantages such as the absence of a guilty conscience at border crossings. Poland also touched on a Crown argument that Singh attempted to mislead a Blue Water Bridge border officer by showing them a photo of a similar load, but not the exact one he was carrying on March 5, 2025, as it was taken one month earlier. But he pointed out the drugs were found in the front of the trailer and if he had taken a photo similar to the one he took in February, which was from the back of the trailer, it wouldn’t have shown the drugs anyway. He also pointed to the long list of things Singh would have had to do in that 37-minute window to get all 281 bricks of cocaine hidden among the sacks of resin. Article content Poland also rejected the Crown’s argument Singh’s moving of the trailer axles in Columbus was indicative he had knowledge. The judge said he was given no information about the load balance when the trailer left the dock and it’s entirely possible it needed to be adjusted irrespective of the cocaine. Poland also said Singh’s evidence did not have any obvious contradictions or inconsistencies and his testimony was capable at least of raising a reasonable doubt of his knowledge. There have been a slew of Blue Water Bridge truck driver drug smuggling trials heard at the Sarnia courthouse in recent years and the majority have ended with convictions, but a trucker with ties to Brampton and Quebec City was also found not guilty two years ago in a $47-million seizure. tbridge@postmedia.com Article content Share this article in your social network Share this Story : Simcoe Reformer Copy Link Email X Reddit Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Comments You must be logged in to join the discussion or read more comments.
